title: TB9-35047
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Burundi.

In 2013, the Appellant joined the Movement for Security and Democracy whose name was later changed to Movement for Solidarity and Democracy (MSD) in which he became a youth leader in his neighbourhood of the capital. He organized and participated in protests banned by the government. In June and July 2015, authorities came looking for him at his home where they beat his family because he had failed to appear after being summoned. After hiding for three months, he fled to Rwanda where he lived for just over two years before coming to Canada using a French passport which was not his.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected his asylum claim essentially because it found the Appellant's testimony misleading regarding travel from Rwanda to Canada, allegations of not being safe in Rwanda were not substantiated by documentary evidence and that he failed to produce or attempt to produce a letter from the Association Burundaise pour la Protection des Droits Humains et des Personnes Détenues (APRDH). The RPD also noted that no written submissions were sent by the Appellant within the delays prescribed in a notice sent to him.

The Appellant submits before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) that the RPD erred regarding notice for accompanying written submissions. It erred in making credibility findings on many aspects that are not internally rational, failed to consider or misapprehended evidence, and further erred by focusing on peripheral matters, being overly microscopic with zeal to find inconsistencies. He submits four documents for consideration as new evidence and requests a hearing before the RAD.
The determinative issue for the RAD is credibility.

I reject the documents submitted as new evidence as well as the request for a hearing before the RAD. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD failed to consider evidence including his passport, not mentioned in the decision, and by drawing a negative inference regarding his credibility because he produced no letter from the APRDH when there actually was one on record. As correctly noted by the Appellant, the RPD ignored evidence of violence committed by Burundian militias in Rwanda. It focused on matters such as the travel itinerary which, while initially relevant, became far more peripheral once the Appellant submitted his passport. However, the evidence which is on the record raises concerns that the Appellant was not given the opportunity to address at the hearing. This precludes me from assessing the credibility of the Appellant with regard to the very core of his asylum claim. For this reason, I find it necessary to send this matter back to the RPD.
The appeal is allowed. I send this matter back to the RPD to be redetermined by a differently constituted panel. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellant is rejected

According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.2

The Appellant submits the following documents for consideration as new evidence before the RAD: i. Affidavit of the Appellant sworn January 8, 2020; ii. Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX sworn January 7, 2020; iii. Information on Addis Ababa Bole International Airport ; and iv. Highlighted National Documentation Package (NDP) Item 10.2.

Document i., the Affidavit of the Appellant, while sworn after the RPD decision, contains evidence which arose prior to it. In fact, this Affidavit merely repeats or paraphrases the evidence given under oath at the hearing. No explanation is provided as to why any information therein was not reasonably available at the time of the decision or could not reasonably have been expected before the decision in the circumstances. In any case, this evidence is not new as it is already on the record before both the RPD and the RAD in the form of both a recording and a transcript.

Document ii., the Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX, is dated after the RPD decision. However, the evidence it contains arose prior to the decision. In fact, this Affidavit confirms that the passport of the Appellant was provided during a break at the hearing and that the RPD then commented that the case appeared to be a good one. All this occurred prior to the RPD decision and no explanation is provided as to why any information therein was not reasonably available at the time of the decision or could not reasonably have been expected before the decision in the circumstances. In any case, the evidence pertaining to the passport is not new as this document is already on the record before both the RPD and the RAD. The opinions expressed by the RPD off record, mid-hearing, before all of the evidence had been heard, are not relevant in this context as they do not create, nor are there allegations of, an apprehension of bias against the Appellant, but actually indicate the contrary.

Document iii., the Information on Addis Ababa Bole International Airport, regardless of the various dates which appear in it, contains evidence which arose prior to the RPD decision, and no explanation is provided as to why any information therein was not reasonably available at the time of the decision or could not reasonably have been expected before the decision in the circumstances. In any case, this evidence does not appear to add to that already on the record before both the RPD and the RAD and thus is not new.
Document iv., the Highlighted NDP Item 10.2, arose prior to the RPD decision and is not new as it is already on the record before both the RPD and the RAD.

For all these reasons, none of this evidence is admitted as new evidence. Since no new evidence has been admitted, section 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) does not allow me to hold a hearing before the RAD.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in part, by failing to consider evidence. I agree with the Appellant in this regard. Most notably, and by way of example, the RPD enumerates a number of documents in a section of its decision titled "Identity". Nowhere in the decision does the RPD ever mention that a passport was submitted, nor does it ever analyze the identity documents which it did acknowledge, and it never reached a conclusion regarding identity. I find that the Appellant has established his identity with his passport.

The RPD very extensively examines the credibility of the Appellant's testimony regarding his itinerary, yet ignores some documents submitted by the Appellant in an attempt to address contradictions. In the absence of any finding that the Appellant has not established his identity or that he was not in his country when he was allegedly there, or that he may have returned to his country, I find that his credibility as pertains to his itinerary to be mostly peripheral. I therefore agree with the Appellant that the RPD focused on peripheral issues.

Also, as correctly noted by the Appellant, the RPD affirms in the decision that violence committed by Burundian authorities in Rwanda is not supported by documentary evidence yet ignores the evidence found at item 10.2 of the NDP, which pertains to this question. While there may be some distinctions to be made between the Appellant and the persons targeted according to this evidence, the failure to address it constitutes an error.

To cite just one more example where the RPD ignored evidence, it specifically made a negative inference regarding the credibility of the Appellant because he produced no letter from the APRDH when there actually was one on record.

I find such errors to be determinative of the appeal. However, I am unable to independently evaluate the credibility of the Appellant as questions central to determining his credibility were not asked at the RPD hearing. By way of example, no questions were put to the Appellant as to why he contends in his BOC form that the party that he joined in 2013 was named the Movement for Security and Democracy and later changed its name although the documentary evidence4 indicates that this name change occurred in 2009 when the party was registered. He was not asked to comment why the card he was issued corresponds to the specimen which ceased being used in 2009 according to the same documentary evidence, especially since he lived in the capital and had a leadership role there for several years. He was never asked why the attestation letter of the MSD issued in December 2017 indicates that he still lived at an address in Burundi at that time although he left that country 2 years earlier and had no intention of returning there. The address in question is not identical to that where he lived in 2015 and therefore would not likely come from party records. Although the Appellant contends that this letter was issued in Rwanda, the address printed on the bottom of the letter is one of a neighbourhood in Bujumbura. The Appellant was not given the opportunity to explain this nor why this assistant to the president would have been satisfied with the Appellant's MSD card although it was issued on a blank that bearded the old name of the party no longer in use for 4 years at the time that he joined the party. The Appellant was not questioned about his activities within the party or his knowledge of the party itself, be it its structure, its program and activities that it held beyond the 2015 protests opposing the 3rd mandate of the president in which several hundred thousand non-party members participated.

These questions are central to determining the credibility of the Appellant and were not asked at the RPD hearing. Section 100(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) does not allow me to hold a hearing on matters unrelated to new evidence admitted. I am thus unable to independently evaluate the credibility of the very core of the asylum claim and therefore find it necessary to return the case to the RPD to be redetermined. In such circumstances, I find it unnecessary to address other errors raised by the Appellant in the memorandum.

The appeal is allowed. I send this matter back to the RPD to be redetermined by a differently constituted panel.
